596.title: Under the fig tree (John 1:43–51)
596.hook: Nathanael scoffs, can anything good come from Nazareth? and is seen before he's met
596.howItsDone: Tradition identifies Nathanael with the apostle Bartholomew, honored on his feast day, and some lectionaries read the call of Nathanael in the season after Epiphany.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two disciples followed, and Jesus asked what they were looking for. Your line was come and see. Who did you invite to something you love? Day five hundred ninety-six.

There's a punchline in this story, and it's a town. Philip has just met Jesus, and he runs to find his friend Nathanael, bursting with it: we've found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about. Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. And Nathanael answers, in the King James words: "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?" A hometown, written off in one line. Nathanael, John tells us later, is from Cana. And Philip doesn't argue. He just borrows Jesus's words from yesterday: come and see.

So Nathanael comes, probably still skeptical. And before he can say a word, Jesus sees him coming and says: "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!" No guile: nothing fake, no hidden angle. Nathanael has just insulted Jesus's hometown, and Jesus compliments his honesty. Nathanael is thrown. How do you know me? And Jesus answers: "Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee." Nobody knows what Nathanael was doing under that fig tree. John doesn't say. Some readers think of the prophets' picture of peace, everyone sitting under their own vine and fig tree. Some point to later Jewish writings that picture teachers studying under fig trees. The honest answer is that we don't know, and that seems to be the point: something private, something only Nathanael would know about, and Jesus saw it. Nathanael's skepticism collapses into a confession: "Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel." And Jesus, almost amused: you believe because I said I saw you under the fig tree? You'll see greater things than these. You'll see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man. That's Jacob's ladder from Genesis, the dream where angels go up and down between heaven and earth. Jacob, who took his brother's blessing by deceit, is echoed in a man with no deceit at all. And the man who made the Nazareth joke ends up seeing heaven open.
screen: `AN ISRAELITE IN WHOM IS NO GUILE.`
`I SAW THEE UNDER THE FIG TREE.`
then, large: `CAN THERE ANY GOOD THING COME OUT OF NAZARETH?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give a place you scorn a chance. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place, a group, or a kind of person you've written off with a joke. A town, a neighborhood, a school, a profession, a political side. Notice the line you usually say about them. Now imagine being taken there by a friend who says, just come and see. Picture one good thing you might find. Hold it a moment. If you pray, you can ask to see people the way Nathanael was seen. The bell holds the time.
Nathanael, whose name means God has given — the skeptic Jesus saw sitting under a fig tree before they ever met, a private moment that turned him into a follower.
Your line: can anything good come? Today, notice when you write off a place or a group, and look for one good thing from there instead. Day five hundred ninety-six.

original.note: Hebrew: Nathanael, 'God has given'. in the New Testament, only John's Gospel names him; the same Hebrew name appears in the Old Testament as Nethaneel.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus had a sort of supernatural vision of a man under a tree.
what it means: a skeptic who mocked Nazareth is seen and known before he's met, and ends up confessing the Son of God.
what a scholar hears: 'no guile' and the angels ascending and descending echo Jacob, who was known for deceit (Genesis 27; 28:12); and what the fig tree meant is genuinely unknown.

597.title: The first sign (John 2:1–12)
597.hook: John calls miracles signs: six stone jars of water become the best wine
597.carry: the best was kept till last
597.howItsDone: Some lectionaries set the wedding at Cana in the weeks after Epiphany, some couples choose it for their weddings, and in the Catholic rosary it is one of the luminous mysteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nathanael, under the fig tree, a skeptic seen before he was met. Your line was can anything good come? What good thing did you find where you didn't expect it? Day five hundred ninety-seven.

The third day, John says, there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee. A wedding, a crowded house, a family hosting everyone they know. And partway through the celebration, the thing no host wants happens. The wine runs out. Jesus is there with his new disciples, and so is his mother. And she's the one who notices. She comes to him and says, simply, in the King James words: "They have no wine." No request. Just the problem, laid in front of her son.

His answer sounds sharp in English: "Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come." But some readers hear more respect in it than English allows, and he uses the same word for her later, from the cross. And his hour keeps coming back in this Gospel, pointing toward the cross and his glory. And his mother doesn't argue. She turns to the servants: "Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it." Nearby stand six stone water jars, set there, John says, for the Jewish rites of purifying, each holding two or three firkins, the King James says. Big jars. Fill them with water, Jesus says, and they fill them to the brim. Draw some out now, and take it to the master of the feast. He tastes it, has no idea where it came from, and calls over the bridegroom: "Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now." Six jars of the best wine, at the end of a party. Then John tells us what kind of story this is: "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him." The King James says miracles, but John's Greek word is sēmeion: sign. Not a show of power for its own sake. A sign. A sign isn't the destination; it points beyond itself. Some Christians have read this one as pointing to abundance, to joy, to a wedding feast at the end of time, to something better saved for last.
screen: then, large: `THOU HAST KEPT THE GOOD WINE UNTIL NOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice something that points beyond itself. Settle, and breathe. Look around wherever you are. Find one ordinary thing: a cup, a ring, a photo, a plant on the windowsill, light on a wall. Let your eyes rest on it. Ask what it points to. A person. A promise. A memory. A hope. Stay with that for a while. An ordinary thing can carry a lot, if you stop long enough to read it. If you pray, you can give thanks for what it points to. The bell holds the time.
Sign. John's word for Jesus's miracles: not just wonders, but things that point beyond themselves, John says, to who Jesus is. Cana is the first.
Your line: the best was kept till last. Today, save something good for the end of the day, and give it to someone else. Day five hundred ninety-seven.

screen: `DAY 597 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TEMPLE OF HIS BODY.`

what it means: the first of John's signs, at a wedding, pointing to glory, abundance and the best saved for last.

598.title: The temple of his body (John 2:13–25)
598.hook: destroy this temple and in three days I'll raise it
598.howItsDone: Some lectionaries set John's account of the temple in Lent, and Paul's words that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit shape Christian teaching about health, rest and the care of the body.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first sign at Cana, and the good wine kept until now. Your line was the best was kept till last. What good thing did you save and give away? Day five hundred ninety-eight.

If you read Luke with us, you already know this scene. Jesus in the temple, driving out the traders. But in Luke it comes at the end, in the last week. John puts it here, in chapter two, right at the start. Christians explain that in different ways. Some think it happened twice, once early and once late. Others think John placed it at the start on purpose, so it would frame the whole story. Either way, it's Passover, the city is full, and Jesus walks into the temple and finds it full of cattle, sheep, doves, and the tables of money changers.
screen: `LUKE PUTS IT LAST; JOHN PUTS IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Some readers point out that the traders were serving pilgrims, who needed animals for the offerings. But Jesus makes a whip of small cords, drives out the sheep and oxen, pours out the coins, and turns over the tables. To the dove sellers he says: "Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise." My Father's house. The leaders ask him for a sign: what gives you the right? And he answers with a riddle: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." They hear it literally, and who wouldn't? "Forty and six years was this temple in building, and wilt thou rear it up in three days?" Then John tells us what the listeners missed: "But he spake of the temple of his body." For Israel, the temple was the place of God's presence among the people. John reads Jesus's riddle this way: that place is now a person, Jesus's own body. Here's the honest part: John says even the disciples didn't get it at the time. Only after he was raised from the dead did they remember he'd said this, and believe. Christians later carried the idea one step further. Paul reminds the church in Corinth that "your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you." So for Paul the body, the ordinary body that gets tired and hungry and sore, is holy ground.
screen: then, large: `BUT HE SPAKE OF THE TEMPLE OF HIS BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for your body as a temple. Settle, and breathe. Start at your feet and slowly move your attention up: legs, back, shoulders, hands, face. Notice where you're tired, or tense, or sore. Don't judge it. Just notice. Then choose one kind thing you'll do for your body today. A glass of water. A walk. An early night. Stretching the place that hurts. Not to fix how you look, but to honor where you live. If you pray, you can give thanks for your body. The bell holds the time.
Naos, the Greek word for the sanctuary, the inner house of God — what John says Jesus meant by destroy this temple: his own body, which would be raised in three days.
Your line: a temple of flesh. Today, do one kind thing for your body, a glass of water, a walk, an early night, as if it were holy ground. Day five hundred ninety-eight.

what it means: a sign that the meeting place of God and people is now a person, his body, destroyed and raised in three days.
what a scholar hears: John uses hieron for the temple courts and naos, sanctuary, for 'this temple'; and he places the scene at the start, unlike the Synoptics.

599.title: Born from above (John 3:1–8)
599.hook: Nicodemus comes by night; the wind blows where it will
599.carry: the wind blows where it will
599.howItsDone: Churches that baptize infants link Jesus's words to Nicodemus with baptism, and in evangelical churches being 'born again' describes a personal commitment to Christ; some Christians hold both together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naos, the temple of his body. Your line was a temple of flesh. What kind thing did you do for your body? Day five hundred ninety-nine.

Some conversations only happen at night. The kitchen at one in the morning. The phone call after everyone's asleep. The question you'd never ask in daylight, in front of people. John tells us about a man who came to Jesus by night. His name is Nicodemus. He's a Pharisee, a respected teacher, a leader among his people. He has a reputation, and he has questions, and he comes in the dark. Maybe to avoid being seen. Maybe for a quiet hour. John doesn't say. But John has already told us the light shines in the darkness.

Nicodemus opens politely: "Rabbi, we know that thou art a teacher come from God." And Jesus answers something he didn't ask: "Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." Here's the key. The Greek word translated again, anōthen, has two meanings. It can mean again, a second time. It can also mean from above. Nicodemus hears the first: "How can a man be born when he is old? can he enter the second time into his mother's womb, and be born?" He's not being foolish; he's taking the words at face value, the way anyone might. But Jesus means the second as well: a birth that comes from God, from above. Born of water and of the Spirit, he says. And then an image from the weather: "The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit." In Greek, the word for wind and the word for Spirit are the same word, pneuma. You can't grab the wind. You can't schedule it. You only hear it in the trees and feel it on your face. Christians understand this new birth in different ways. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican teaching connects born of water and the Spirit closely with baptism. Evangelical preaching speaks of being born again as a personal turning to Christ, often a moment a person can name. Both read Jesus as pointing to a life that starts from God, like wind you can hear but not hold.
screen: `HOW CAN A MAN BE BORN WHEN OLD?`
then, large: `THE WIND BLOWETH WHERE IT LISTETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel the wind. If you can, step outside or open a window. If not, just notice the air moving in the room, or your own breath. Settle. Feel the air touch your face, your hands. Listen for it: in leaves, against a window, in a distant hum. You can't see it, and you can't hold it, but it's plainly there. Breathe it in slowly. If you pray, you can ask God's Spirit to move in you like that. If you don't, simply let the air remind you that some things are real without being held. The bell holds the time.
Anothen, the Greek word that means both from above and again — Jesus's double meaning for Nicodemus: a second birth that comes from God, by water and the Spirit, as free as the wind.
Your line: the wind blows where it will. Today, when you feel a breeze, stop for one breath and notice it before you move on. Day five hundred ninety-nine.

600.title: For God so loved (John 3:9–21)
600.hook: the most famous verse: God so loved the world
600.carry: not to condemn but to save
600.howItsDone: John 3:16 is among the first verses many Christians memorize as children, and many churches read John 3:14–21 in Lent, pairing it with the story of the bronze serpent in Numbers 21.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anothen, born from above, and Nicodemus in the dark. Your line was the wind blows where it will. Where did you stop and feel it? Day six hundred. Six hundred days on the path.

You've probably seen it without reading it. Painted on a sign at a football game. Printed on the bottom of a fast-food cup. Written on an athlete's eye black. Just a reference: John three sixteen. For many people it's the one Bible verse they could find without looking it up. Which makes it easy to stop hearing. Today we put it back where it lives, in the middle of a conversation at night, with a confused teacher named Nicodemus, and read the verse around it, the one that hardly anyone puts on a sign.

Nicodemus is still asking, how can these things be? And Jesus reaches for a story Nicodemus knew well. In the wilderness, when the people were dying of snakebite, Moses lifted up a bronze serpent on a pole, and whoever looked at it lived. "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up." In John, lifted up has a double meaning too: raised on a cross, and raised in glory. Then the famous lines, in the King James words: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. For God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world; but that the world through him might be saved." Two things to notice. First, the little word so. In Greek it's houtōs, and many scholars point out it means in this way more than so much. God loved the world in this way: by giving. Second, the world. John's word is kosmos, and in his Gospel the world is often the part of creation that has turned away from God. That's what God loved. Not the lovable parts. The world. And then verse seventeen, the one that rarely gets painted on signs: not to condemn, but to save. A small honest note: Greek has no quotation marks, so nobody knows exactly where Jesus's words end and John's reflection begins in this passage. Red-letter Bibles disagree about it. Christians read these verses as the whole Gospel in miniature: love that gives, aimed at a world that doesn't deserve it, not to condemn it, but to save.
screen: then, large: `FOR GOD SO LOVED THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read John three sixteen and seventeen. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, find them, or simply listen. Settle, and breathe. Read sixteen slowly, out loud if you can. Then read seventeen, just as slowly. Not to condemn the world, but that the world through him might be saved. Let the second verse sit next to the first. Then think of one part of the world you find hardest to love. A person, a group, a place. Hold it inside those two verses for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Kosmos, the Greek word for the world, the ordered universe — John's word for what God loved in this way, by giving his Son, not to condemn, but to save.
Your line: not to condemn but to save. Today, when you're about to judge someone, ask what it would look like to help instead. Day six hundred.

601.title: He must increase (John 3:22–36)
601.hook: the Baptist, happy to fade: he must increase, I must decrease
601.howItsDone: Churches in the West and East keep the birth of John the Baptist on June 24, near midsummer in the northern hemisphere, and 'he must increase, but I must decrease' is quoted by some Christians as a motto for humble service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kosmos, the world God so loved, read inside its night conversation. Your line was not to condemn but to save. When did you choose to help instead of judge? Day six hundred one.

A band, a small business, a church plant: anyone who has started one may know the day when someone new arrives and the crowds start drifting over. That's where John the Baptist is now. He's still baptizing, at a place called Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there. And Jesus, not far away, is baptizing too. Well, his disciples are; John's Gospel adds a little later that Jesus himself didn't baptize. John's followers come to him worried, almost hurt: Rabbi, the one you pointed to across the Jordan, he's baptizing, and everyone is going to him.

John's answer starts with a sentence that would settle a lot of jealousy, in the King James words: "A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven." Whatever you have, you were given. Then he reminds them: I told you, I'm not the Christ, I was sent ahead of him. And then a picture from a wedding. The groom is the one with the bride. The best man, the friend of the bridegroom, isn't jealous. He stands there listening for the groom's voice, and when he hears it, he's overjoyed. "This my joy therefore is fulfilled." Then the line that gives today its name: "He must increase, but I must decrease." Must. Not a sad must, the way you'd talk about getting older. A glad one, the way you'd talk about a child growing taller than you. His whole work was pointing, and now people are going where he pointed. That's what success looks like for a pointer. Augustine of Hippo, preaching on John the Baptist's feast, noticed something about this line. The feast of John's birth falls near midsummer, after which the days get shorter. Christmas falls near midwinter, after which the days get longer. He must increase; I must decrease, written, Augustine says, into the calendar and the sunlight. The chapter closes with words, whether John the Baptist's or the Gospel writer's, about the one who comes from above: the Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.
screen: `A GLAD MUST, NOT A SAD ONE.`
then, large: `HE MUST INCREASE, BUT I MUST DECREASE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let someone else shine. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose star is rising near you. A younger colleague. A sibling. A friend whose project is taking off. Someone who might, honestly, make you a little jealous. Picture them succeeding. Notice whatever you feel: pride, envy, both. Don't scold yourself. Then try the best man's posture: standing beside them, listening, glad. Think of one thing you could do this week to help their light grow. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Bridegroom, the one the best man serves without envy — John the Baptist's picture for Jesus, as the crowds left him: joy, not rivalry, like hearing the groom's voice.
Your line: this my joy is fulfilled. Today, step back and let someone else take the credit, the spotlight or the last word, and be glad about it. Day six hundred one.

602.title: The Samaritan woman (John 4:1–26)
602.hook: a well, a thirsty Jew, a woman with five husbands, and worship in spirit and truth
602.howItsDone: Some lectionaries set this story in Lent; the Orthodox Church honors the woman as Saint Photini, and her conversation is used to teach that worship isn't bound to one place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John the Baptist watched the crowds drift toward Jesus and called himself the friend of the bridegroom, glad to fade. Your line was this my joy is fulfilled. Who did you let shine? Day six hundred two.

Midday, by the usual reading of John's clock. A well outside a Samaritan town called Sychar, and a tired man sitting on the edge of it, alone, because his friends have gone to buy food. John says it plainly: "Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well: and it was about the sixth hour." Then a woman comes with her jar. And the tired man, a Jewish teacher in Samaritan country, does something she doesn't expect. He asks her for a drink.

She's as surprised as anyone: "How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans." Jews and Samaritans were neighbors divided over where God should be worshiped, and she'll name it herself in a moment: our fathers worshiped on this mountain, and you say Jerusalem. Jesus answers with a riddle about water. If you knew who was asking, you'd have asked him, and he'd have given you living water. Some readers point out that living water could also mean plain running water, fresh from a spring, and she takes him literally. You have nothing to draw with, she says, and the well is deep. Then he turns the talk to her life. Go, call your husband. I have no husband, she says. True, he answers: you've had five, and the man you're with now isn't your husband. Some preachers have called her a sinner. The text never says why she had five husbands. Widowhood, divorce, something else: John is silent, and some readers now hear in her story more loss than scandal. She doesn't run. She asks the question that divided their peoples: which mountain is the right one? And Jesus says an hour is coming when it won't be this mountain or Jerusalem. "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth." Then he says plainly who he is. "I that speak unto thee am he." He says it to a Samaritan woman whose name John never gives. This week we've sat under a fig tree, tasted the best wine last, watched a temple turned into a body, heard about wind and a new birth, God so loving the world, a friend glad to fade, and now a well at noon.
screen: then, large: `IN SPIRIT AND IN TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: worship without a building today. Wherever you are right now is the well. A kitchen, a car, a bench. Settle, and breathe. Notice that nothing about this place is holy in the usual way. Then let the two words sit with you. Spirit: what's alive in you right now, under the noise. Truth: one honest thing about your life you'd usually leave out. If you pray, you can bring both, just as they are, to God, here, without a church around you. If you don't, simply be honest and awake for these minutes. The bell holds the time.
Living water, what Jesus offers an unnamed woman at the well, who takes it at first for plain water from a spring, before she hears him say plainly who he is.
Your line: in spirit and in truth. Today, find one ordinary place, a sink or a sidewalk, and treat it as a place for spirit and truth. Day six hundred two, and another week on the path.

original.note: Greek: living water. the phrase could also mean fresh running water from a spring, and she hears it that way.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a sinful woman Jesus forgave.
what it means: a long, serious conversation across a deep divide, ending with Jesus saying plainly who he is.
what a scholar hears: "living water" can also mean running water, and John never explains the five husbands, so the scandal may be more ours than the text's.
